title: An additive approach for the optimal solution of the prize-collecting traveling salesman problem
contribution: First exact algorithm for the prize-collecting TSP, built on a family of bounds from assignment and 1-arborescence substructures chained additively through reduced-cost residual instances (p. 25).
problem_entry: PC-TSP generalizes the TSP and the min-form 0-1 knapsack, arises in supplier selection and steel rolling-mill scheduling, had no optimal algorithm; entry is bound quality since available relaxations do not dominate one another (pp. 23, 25).
key_idea: Several ILP models expose assignment and 1-arborescence substructures; their Lagrangian bounds, a disjunction bound and an instance-shrinking transformation (ADD1) are chained additively, each passing a residual instance to the next (pp. 4, 5, 6, 7, 18-20, 22).
assumptions: Directed complete graph, arc costs, vertex prizes, penalties, prize goal g; nonnegative costs, no triangle inequality; random classes A, B, C with n = 20-100, zero penalties (pp. 10, 17, 25).
proof_devices: validity of additive chain by induction from v(I^(h)) ≥ 0 and δ^(h) + v(I^(h)) ≤ v(I) (pp. 4, 22)
residual costs from LP duals of assignment and arborescence problems (pp. 5, 6, 20)
transformation validity by solution mapping and shortcutting repeated visits (p. 19)
experiments: Five instances per cell, bounds as ratio to LB1 with VAX 11/780 seconds (p. 10); B&B times, nodes (p. 15); n = 120-200 on VAX 8650 (p. 12); no exact rival (p. 25).
positioning: First exact method for PC-TSP; one application of the Fischetti–Toth additive approach next to ATSP, MDVSP and STSP papers (pp. 22, 25).
writing: Bounds reported as ratios to a reference bound per class and size; numeric tables lost in OCR (p. 10).
limits_future: LB4/LB5 gains shrink as α → 1; class B hard from near-equal solutions; future: ad hoc branching, dominance criteria, reductions (pp. 11, 12, 15).

method_links.note: Aggregation as a relaxation device: ADD1 collapses zero-reduced-cost subtours and compresses costs by shortest paths, aggregate-then-bound logic of orbital shrinking (my reading), used to break bound saturation inside an additive chain; authors name the loss of information and keep the depot's subtour unshrunk.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: bounds from different substructures chained through reduced-cost residual instances, validity from two conditions; same approach applied to ATSP, MDVSP, STSP
several models written to expose the assignment and arborescence substructures, each yielding a Lagrangian bound; also S060, S069, S114

transferable: Combine relaxations that do not dominate one another by passing the reduced-cost matrix of one as the costs of the next; prove the chain valid once, from v(residual) ≥ 0 and bound + v(residual) ≤ v(instance) (p. 4).
Seed a scalar Lagrangian multiplier with the dual of a continuous knapsack whose item costs are lower bounds on the extra cost of serving each item (p. 5).
When a bound saturates on zero-cost structures, shrink them to single nodes and re-solve, leaving unshrunk the structure most likely to contain the optimum (pp. 7, 18).
Report every bound as a ratio to one reference bound, with its time, per instance class and size (p. 10).

quotes.text: Since none of these bounds dominates the others, a possible way to obtain a strengthened bound is to compute the maximum among them.
Analysis of other possible sequences of bounding procedures is not reported, since the higher computing times are generally not rewarded by significant improvements in the bound quality.

title: The symmetric generalized traveling salesman polytope
contribution: Dimension, facet and non-facet results for the GTSP and E-GTSP polytopes, with two lifting procedures that turn every TSP facet into a GTSP / E-GTSP facet (pp. 4, 23).
problem_entry: GTSP and E-GTSP as non-spanning TSP variants combining selection and sequencing; entry ties their polytopes to the TSP polytope Q, a face of the GTSP polytope P (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Intermediate polytopes P(F) with fixed y_v; releasing a node raises dimension by at most one, so TSP facets lift sequentially (Thm 2.1-2.2, pp. 5-6); GSECs in sparse E(S) form, generalized combs, fan inequalities, E-GTSP facets by induction on n − m (pp. 8-13, 19-23).
assumptions: Complete undirected graph, nodes partitioned into m clusters (lower bound 5 on m), binary edge and node variables, model (1.1)-(1.7); GTSP = E-GTSP under triangle inequality (pp. 2-4).
proof_devices: dimension by induction on |F| with affinely independent tours (Theorem 2.1, pp. 5-6)
Padberg's sequential lifting (Theorem 2.2, p. 6)
rank of the v-compatibility graph (Lemma 3.1, p. 13)
tight-triangular inequalities with a three-edge exchange (Lemma 3.2, p. 14)
tight solutions drawn for an ad hoc case (Theorem 3.8, p. 19)
parametric lift to full rank with worked example (pp. 21-23)
positioning: Polyhedral half of the GTSP project; companion branch-and-cut solves up to 442 nodes (pp. 1, 4); preliminary version EURO XII/TIMS XXXI 1992 (p. 5).
writing: Theorem-proof preprint; sparser constraint form motivated as more suitable for cutting planes (p. 9).
limits_future: No limits or future work stated; text ends with the lifting procedure (p. 23).

method_links.note: Era: only trivial thinning (intra-cluster edges dropped, p. 12) plus a sparser constraint form (p. 9); the substance is strengthening a natural model by facets, the reflex Method 1 later defines itself against. Pre-2003 practice, not a reversal of a stated view.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Reduce to the known special case and lift
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the TSP polytope as a face, a one-dimension-per-node step, every known facet lifted; for E-GTSP nodes added to clusters one at a time

transferable: To study the polytope of a generalization, interpolate between it and the known polytope by fixing variables (P(F)), prove that each released variable raises the dimension by at most one, and lift known facets along any sequence, noting that different sequences give different facets (pp. 5–7).
Before separating a cut family, use the problem's equations to rewrite it in its sparsest equivalent form (p. 9).
For facet proofs in a clustered generalization, induct on n − m: the face of the restriction plus a rank argument on a compatibility graph (p. 13).
coauthors: Juan José Salazar González, Paolo Toth

quotes.text: The theoretical results herein described were used by Fischetti, Salazar and Toth [5] to design a branch-and-cut algorithm for the exact solution of instances with up to 442 nodes.
As a consequence, every facet of the TSP polytope (associated with a graph with m nodes) can be lifted to a facet of the E-GTSP polytope

title: Exact and approximate algorithms for the index selection problem in physical database design
contribution: Shows the NP-hard index selection problem is solvable in practice: exact LP-based branch-and-cut for several hundred indexes and queries, Lagrangian heuristic with error bound for several thousand (abstract, p. 2).
problem_entry: Choose indexes minimizing workload cost under a memory bound; heuristics give no optimality estimate and exact methods are complete enumeration (p. 2).
key_idea: 0-1 ILP generalizing KP and UPLP; branch on fractional y only, strengthened at run time by x_ij ≤ y_j and knapsack covers; LP-guided heuristics, reductions, Lagrangian decomposition by relation (pp. 4-10).
assumptions: Known data allocation, at most one index per relation per query, separable joins, update costs independent of access path; no restriction on cost functions; NP-hard even without memory bound (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: ADDCUTS: all violated x_ij ≤ y_j else one most violated cover, dual simplex re-optimization (p. 7)
cover separation by knapsack on fractional y after fixing integral ones (p. 7)
heuristic H2 bucket of 2v + 1 indexes around the critical index (p. 8)
Lagrangian error bound GAP(λ) with binary-search-like λ rule (p. 10)
experiments: Random instances simulating real databases, 10-20 relations, 10 per cell, avg/worst time, nodes, root gap; ablation S-BAB without cuts fails on every instance; Lagrangian heuristic up to 1,000 relations (pp. 10-12).
positioning: Off-field Bologna application from Caprara's 1991 Laurea thesis (pp. 2, 13-14).
writing: Worst cases printed next to averages; ablation arm of the same code (pp. 10-11).
limits_future: Relaxing assumptions a)-c) needs specific algorithms; future: object-oriented and knowledge-base systems, methods for extended models (p. 12).

method_links.note: Step 1, practice, joint: the comparison arm is the authors' own code with one component switched off (S-BAB, separation of (9) and (10) inhibited), on the same data set, so the arms share all other machinery.

Steps 1 and 5, practice, joint: reductions remove on average more than 30% of candidate indexes before branching; the subtraction test removes both cut classes at once and shows they must stay, not one ingredient at a time.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: the problem is recognized as a generalization of KP and UPLP, and each substructure contributes its cut family

transferable: List the classical problems your model contains as special cases (here KP when every query gains from one index only, UPLP without the memory bound) and import each one's cuts, separated at run time (pp. 4, 6–7).
Separate covers on the fractional variables only: fix items at value 1 into the cover and items at value 0 out, then solve the small knapsack exactly (p. 7).
Judge a cut family by an ablation run of the same code with that separator inhibited, on the same instances (p. 11).
Turn the Lagrangian penalty into an a posteriori error bound for the heuristic solution and report it per instance class (pp. 10–12).
Print worst cases next to averages in every table cell (pp. 10–11).

quotes.text: Since we had no access to real-world ISP instances with a significantly large number of relations, we decided to validate the performance of our algorithm on random instances.
For all instances S-BAB did not succeed in finding a provably optimal solution, and ran out of memory after having generated and solved more than 10,000 branch-decision nodes.

title: Experiments with a multi-commodity formulation for the symmetric capacitated vehicle routing problem
contribution: A three-index vehicle-flow formulation for the symmetric CVRP whose per-vehicle decomposition of fractional solutions supports new inequality families (p. 2).
problem_entry: Symmetric CVRP; prior exact work (Fisher, Laporte–Nobert–Desrochers, Cornuéjols–Harche, identical-demand B&C) all uses two-index O(n²) models (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Per-vehicle copies of edge and node variables, O(n²m), letting fractional solutions decompose into cycle problems; families (9)-(12) including lifted capacity, path and cover inequalities, plus symmetry-breaking (13)-(14) (pp. 2-4).
assumptions: m identical vehicles of capacity Q, one depot, positive demands, symmetric costs, at most m routes; x^k_e ∈ {0,1,2} on depot edges (pp. 1-2).
proof_devices: max-flow separation of (10) on a graph with n + 2 vertices, dominating large multistar inequalities (p. 4)
heuristic separation of f = 1 family (p. 4)
bin-packing bound on vehicle count then fixing depot visits (p. 4)
positioning: Companion of the authors' additive branch-and-bound for the asymmetric CVRP (p. 1).
writing: Model and inequality families only, no computational section despite the title (p. 4).
limits_future: Trade-off of more variables for decomposable fractional solutions (p. 2); no conclusion, limits or future work (p. 4).

method_links.note: Era: the model is deliberately fattened (vehicle index, O(n²m) instead of O(n²)) to strengthen the LP, and the vehicle symmetry is broken by ordering constraints; both reflexes Method 1 (thin first) and H1 later invert. A 1995 practice predating the method's first statement (2003).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: per-vehicle knapsack constraints yield covers, the per-vehicle cycle decomposition yields path inequalities

transferable: When a per-vehicle (per-commodity) index lets fractional solutions decompose into per-vehicle structures, separate per-vehicle inequalities, and break the index symmetry by requiring that vehicles with smaller indices visit clients with smaller indices (pp. 2, 4).
Bound the number of vehicles by bin packing before the search and fix the depot visit of that many vehicles (p. 4).
coauthors: Juan José Salazar González, Paolo Toth

quotes.text: it allows us to decompose the fractional solution of CVRP into the fractional solutions of particular cycle problems, and therefore to consider additional inequalities to strengthen the LP-relaxation

In order to avoid equivalent solutions obtained by interchanging the third index, it is useful to introduce a convenient renumeration of the clients, so that vehicles with smaller indices visit clients with smaller indices.

title: Experiments with Controlled Rounding for Statistical Disclosure Control in Tabular Data with Linear Constraints
Solution of large-scale railway crew planning problems: The Italian experience
contribution: Reports the ALPI crew planning system for Italian railways: a three-phase decomposition with a Lagrangian set-covering heuristic on a priced core and a Lagrangian-bound rostering heuristic, on instances up to a million pairings (pp. 4-14).
problem_entry: EU deregulation pushes FS to computer crew planning; instances reach 5,000 trips and 1,000,000 pairings; academic entry via FS/AIRO competitions FASTER and FARO won by DEIS Bologna (pp. 1-7).
key_idea: Pairing generation, set-covering optimization by the Caprara–Fischetti–Toth Lagrangian heuristic on a priced core, and rostering by a constructive heuristic guided by a disjoint-circuit assignment bound (pp. 4-11).
assumptions: Set covering not partitioning since crews may deadhead; inclusion-maximal pairings only; per-depot base constraints; cyclic 6-day-week rosters under union rules (pp. 6-10).
proof_devices: depth-first pairing enumeration with simple bounds (p. 7)
aggressive subgradient step-size policy (p. 8)
core kept open by pricing (p. 9)
two pairs of multipliers / assignment problems for tight rostering bound (p. 11)
refining by rebuilding last rosters with perturbed parameters (p. 11)
experiments: CFT optimal/best on 92 of 94 literature instances, 6 of 22 open improved; 7 FS instances vs other codes tested by FS, mean gap 0.9%; 36 rostering instances, 26 optimal; one integrated feedback run 46→44 weeks (pp. 12-14).
positioning: Railway-codes period with Ferrovie dello Stato, written at Udine; application entered through public challenges (pp. 1, 5).
writing: Industrial experience report mapping the planners' process (p. 5).
limits_future: Sequential approach not globally optimal (p. 5); ALPI delayed by reorganization; ≥1% driver savings; future: feedback between phases 2 and 3 (p. 14).

method_links.note: Practice, joint, before 2000: spread between near-equivalent runs used as a resource; greedy applied to many near-optimal multiplier vectors since the bound does not predict solution quality, rostering refinement perturbs parameters at random; diversity from dual vectors, not seeds, exploited without measurement (no placebo arm, no seed table).
Steps 1-2, practice, joint: covering chosen over partitioning so dominated columns need not be generated, and a priced core of low Lagrangian-cost columns replaces the full million-column problem.
The rival column of Table 1 is FS's own test of other set-covering codes, with AIRO members attending evaluation tests, an external harness; rivals' machines and limits not given.

transferable: In a Lagrangian heuristic, run the primal greedy for many near-optimal multiplier vectors, not only the best one, and keep the best primal solution (p. 8).
For a set-covering problem with a million columns, work on a core of the lowest Lagrangian-cost columns and keep it open with pricing (pp. 8–9).
If over-covering is allowed, generate only inclusion-maximal columns among those of equal cost (p. 6).
In a phased decomposition, feed the downstream phase's difficulties back into the upstream costs and iterate, recording the objective at each iteration (pp. 12, 14).
coauthors: Alberto Caprara, Pier Luigi Guida, Paolo Toth, Daniele Vigo

quotes.text: In addition, no strict correlation exists between the lower bound value L(u) and the quality of the SCP solution found. Therefore, it is worthwhile applying the heuristic procedure for several near-optimal Lagrangian multiplier vectors.
The above three-step approach was implemented due to its relatively low development risk, and also because it maps fairly well the process currently followed by the planners.

title: Models and algorithms for the 2-dimensional cell suppression problem in statistical disclosure control
contribution: A one-binary-per-cell model with max-flow-separated capacity cuts and five further inequality families, in a branch-and-cut that solves 2-D tables with 250,000 cells and about 10,000 sensitive cells exactly (pp. 1, 5-12, 29-30).
problem_entry: Strongly NP-hard secondary cell suppression for 2-D tables; earlier work heuristic, Kelly's MILP has 20M variables and 30M constraints, Geurts' model solved at most 20 × 6 (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Protection levels hold iff every relevant cut of the incremental network has enough capacity: capacity constraints by max-flow with tightened coefficients, plus bridge, comb/matching, lifted cover, 2-edge cover and path inequalities (pp. 5-12).
assumptions: 2-D table with marginals, nonnegative weights, lower/upper protection levels, attacker bounds typically [0,0] or [0,+∞]; MW-BSP relaxation valid for inclusion-minimal solutions (pp. 3-4, 8).
proof_devices: Padberg–Rinaldi branch-and-cut (p. 13)
parametric max-flow preprocessing (p. 13)
cut management rules: capacity cuts first, ≤100 cuts per round, separator off after 5 failures (p. 14)
matching cuts as {0, 1/2}-CG cuts by minimum odd cut (p. 15)
covers by MT1R after fixing (p. 16)
LP-guided shortest-path heuristic with (1 − x*) w weights (pp. 18-19)
strong branching on 5 candidates (p. 19)
validity by Chvátal–Gomory derivations with multipliers 1/2 and parity (pp. 9, 12)
experiments: ANSI C, Pentium/200, CPLEX 3.0; 49 SDC Library + 9 office instances + 3 random generators, 3,600 s limit, per-family cut counts; SDC Library under 1 s vs Geurts' thousands of seconds; 45 of 550 KGA instances unsolved, mean gap 0.27% (pp. 19-22).
positioning: SDC line inside the 1996-1999 ESPRIT SDC project; details in a May 1997 Padova report (pp. 1, 21, 30).
writing: Per-family cut counts per instance class; failures printed with gap and cause (pp. 21-22).
limits_future: Larger Benedetti tables not tried (p. 21); future: new inequality classes, bridgeless subgraph polyhedron, multidimensional tables (p. 30).

method_links.note: Step 3, practice, joint: against Kelly's 20-million-variable model, attacker flow variables are dropped and replaced by exponentially many capacity cuts separated by max-flow. My reading: projects flows into cut form, the Benders-type move of the later facility-location redesign; the paper does not use the word Benders.

Dated lapse, 1999: the Geurts comparison uses times published for a SUN Sparc 1+ against runs on a PC Pentium/200; the gap dwarfs any machine factor but the arms do not share machinery. The skill lists the same lapse for 2017.
Step 6: failures within the time limit are printed with their gap and a cause.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Chvátal–Gomory derivation as validity proof and separation handle
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: combs and path inequalities proved valid by {0, 1/2} derivations, matching cuts separated as {0, 1/2}-cuts; see S139
a bridgeless-subgraph relaxation for bridge and comb cuts, the knapsack reading of each capacity cut for covers

transferable: Replace auxiliary flow variables by the cut constraints that max-flow/min-cut duality gives on the decision variables, separate them exactly by max-flow, and cap each coefficient at the right-hand side (pp. 5–6, 14).
Read every generated cut αx ≥ α0 on 0-1 variables as a knapsack, and separate lifted covers only from the cuts in the current LP and the pool (pp. 10, 15–16).

Cut-loop defaults worth copying: separate the cheap exact family first, stop at the first family with violations, cap the cuts per round, and switch off a separator after k consecutive failures (p. 14).
Get two cuts from each max-flow by taking the inclusion-minimal and the inclusion-maximal minimum cut (p. 14).
Bias a primal heuristic with LP values by multiplying each weight by (1 − x*) and removing the arcs fixed to 0 (p. 19).
Report per-family cut counts per instance class; they show where a family plays no role (combs on the Benedetti class, p. 21; covers on general tables, p. 22).

quotes.text: Although the model contains an exponential number of capacity constraints, its linear programming relaxation can still be solved efficiently by using a run-time constraint generation technique.

Based on our computational experience, in order to save computing time we decided to inhibit any separation procedure (except that for capacity cut constraints) failing to produce violated cuts after 5 consecutive calls.

title: On the Separation of Maximally Violated mod-k Cuts
contribution: Separation theory for maximally violated mod-k Chvátal–Gomory cuts by Gaussian elimination in GF(k), an O(|E*||V|²) TSP separation via necklaces, and new facet-defining mod-k TSP cuts (pp. 4-10).
problem_entry: Exact polynomial separation known for few TSP facet classes and no comb class; ABCC's maximally violated combs and Fleischer–Tardos for planar support; {0,1/2}-separation NP-hard; carry the idea to mod k and general ILPs (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Mod-k cuts are CG cuts with multipliers in {0, 1/k, …}; violation ≤ (k − 1)/k, and maximally violated ones solve a congruence system on tight rows with θ = k − 1, by Gaussian elimination for prime k; TSP needs only beads and dominoes of O(|V|) necklaces (Thms 1-7, pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Any ILP with integer A, b, P_I ≠ P and given x* ∈ P; known prime factorization of k; for TSP degree equations, SECs and nonnegativity (pp. 1, 3-5).
proof_devices: scaling multipliers by w ∈ {2, …, k − 1} in GF(k) (Theorem 2, p. 4)
reduction modulo a prime factor (Theorem 3, p. 5)
replacing a tight SEC by tight constraints agreeing mod k (Theorem 4, pp. 6-7)
cactus and necklace structure of tight sets (pp. 5-6)
positioning: Chvátal rank-1 separation line after Caprara–Fischetti {0,1/2}-cuts, before MIP separation over the first Chvátal closure (Method 6) (p. 2).
writing: IPCO extended abstract; proofs of Theorems 6-7 and ATSP results left to the full paper (pp. 8-10).
limits_future: Future: undominated mod-k TSP cuts, other problems, practical use of the separation (p. 10).

method_links.note: The separation sub-decision is written as an integer program in the multipliers but solved exactly only in its maximally violated special case by linear algebra in GF(k), not by a general-purpose solver; nothing implemented, a counter-case to the skill's taste warning against an algorithm without implementation and test (practical use left open, p. 10).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Restrict separation to maximally violated cuts
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: an NP-hard separation becomes a linear congruence system once only cuts violated by (k − 1)/k are sought

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Chvátal–Gomory derivation as validity proof and separation handle
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: mod-k derivations define the family, Theorem 4 swaps derivation rows mod k, extended combs shown to be mod-2 cuts; see S069

transferable: When the separation problem of a Chvátal–Gomory family is NP-hard, look for maximally violated members only: drop every row with positive slack, fix the right-hand-side residue to k − 1 and solve the congruence system by Gaussian elimination modulo a prime (p. 4).
Shrink the row set before solving by using the combinatorial structure of the tight constraints (here necklaces of tight sets: O(|V|) rows instead of O(|V|²), pp. 5–8).
To show that a known inequality family belongs to a cut class, exhibit its derivation with explicit multipliers (p. 9).

quotes.text: However, finding a maximally violated mod-k cut amounts to finding any feasible solution of the congruence system (2)–(4) after having fixed θ = k − 1 and having removed all the rows of (A, b) associated with a strictly positive slack
Furthermore, the practical use of the separation methods herein proposed should be investigated.
